vignette: He sits on the edge of the therapy chair, shoulders hunched forward as if bracing for impact. His hands rest on his knees, fingers tracing the same circular path over his knuckles. At sixty-two, he carries himself with the measured precision of a man who has spent decades making split-second decisions in operating rooms, yet his breathing remains shallow, restricted to the upper chest. He tells the story the way it unfolded, though the retelling still tightens the muscles in his jaw. It begins on a Tuesday in November, three years ago. He drives home from the hospital, the city slick with rain, his mind still replaying a difficult abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. The semi-truck runs the red light at the intersection of Elm and Fourth. The world collapses into glass, twisted steel, and the deafening roar of crumpling metal. He sees the sudden silence after the impact, the smell of coolant and burnt rubber, the way the steering column pins his left leg until firefighters cut him free. His wife, Elena, finds him in the emergency bay, her face pale beneath the flashing lights. In the weeks that follow, he wakes gasping in his own bed, drenched in sweat, convinced the steering wheel is about to crush his ribs. The house that once feels like a sanctuary now requires constant scanning of the windows, the driveway, the street beyond the fence. He stops sleeping past four in the morning. When he tries to lie still, his mind replays the impact on a loop, each time with the sickening certainty that it is happening again. He begins taking back roads to the hospital, navigating winding alleys he has never used before, his eyes fixed on the brake pedal the moment he enters any vehicle. He tells the hospital administration he needs a brief leave, though the truth is harder to voice: he is afraid he will never be steady enough to pick up a scalpel again. When he finally returns to the OR, the transition fractures. The sterile scent of antiseptic used to ground him; now it triggers a cold knot in his stomach. He stands at the scrub sink for nearly ten minutes, watching his hands under the water, checking for tremors that are not there, then again, when they are. He avoids the highway on-call routes, taking the long way to trauma bays, which means running late to his own surgeries. He begins double-checking instrument counts three times, a habit that draws quiet questions from his scrub techs. At home, Elena asks how his day went, and he gives her the clinical summary he gives to patients—stable vitals, clean margins, uncomplicated recovery—while the interior of his chest feels like concrete. He stops initiating conversation after dinner. He sleeps in the guest room, not out of irritation, but because the sound of her breathing in the next bed sometimes pulls him back to the passenger seat where she sat in the car that night, and the memory of her blood on the dashboard is too sharp to bear. He and Elena speak in Spanish when the house is quiet, a language that once softened their days but now feels heavy with everything left unspoken. He is back at work now, leading a cardiovascular rotation, yet his days are measured in careful calculations and near misses. He notices how other drivers brake too suddenly and jerks his own wheel without meaning to. He catches himself counting the exits in every restaurant, every conference room, every hospital corridor. He tells his wife he is fine, but his hands no longer feel entirely his own when he reaches for her. The operating theater remains the one place where the noise fades, where the rhythm of the monitors and the weight of his responsibilities push the past into the periphery, if only for a few hours. He walks to the hospital parking garage each morning, taps the roof of his car with two fingers, and takes a long, slow breath before pressing the unlock button.
